extracted.intended_audience: Authors, peer reviewers, editors, and journal staff involved in medical journal publishing
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and requirements for disclosing financial and non-financial relationships, activities, and conflicts of interest for participants in the medical journal publication process (authors, reviewers, editors). Covers what to disclose, how to report funding and data access, recusal, and use of the ICMJE Disclosure Form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of relationships and activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Public trust in the scientific process and the credibility of published articles depend in part on how transparently an author’s relationships and activities, directly or topically related to a work, are handled during the planning, implementation, writing, peer review, editing, and publication of scientific work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should provide complete disclosures so readers can judge whether relationships/activities are pertinent to a paper. Complete disclosure demonstrates commitment to transparency and maintains trust in the scientific process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of conflict of interest (COI) and role of perceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The potential for conflict of interest and bias exists when professional judgment concerning a primary interest (such as patients' welfare or the validity of research) may be influenced by a secondary interest (such as financial gain). Perceptions of conflict of interest are as important as actual conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize both actual and perceived conflicts; when in doubt, disclose. The presence of a relationship or activity does not always indicate problematic influence, but perception can erode trust as much as actual conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial relationships to disclose (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Financial relationships (such as employment, consultancies, stock ownership or options, honoraria, patents, and paid expert testimony) are the most easily identifiable, the ones most often judged to represent potential conflicts of interest and thus the most likely to undermine the credibility of the journal, the authors, and of science itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List specific financial ties (employment, consultancies, equity, honoraria, patents, paid testimony, etc.). Treat these as likely relevant COIs and disclose accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-financial interests to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Other interests may also represent or be perceived as conflicts, such as personal relationships or rivalries, academic competition, and intellectual beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose significant non-financial relationships/activities that could bias or be perceived to bias the work; these should not be overlooked simply because they are not monetary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding restrictive sponsor agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must avoid entering into agreements with study sponsors, both for-profit and non-profit, that interfere with authors’ access to all of the study’s data or that interfere with their ability to analyze and interpret the data and to prepare and publish manuscripts independently when and where they choose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies that dictate where authors may publish their work violate academic freedom. Journals may require authors to provide sponsor agreements in confidence to verify compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to report as misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Purposeful failure to report those relationships or activities specified on the journal’s disclosure form is a form of misconduct, as is discussed in section III.B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate omission of required disclosures can be treated as research/publication misconduct; respondents should follow journal sanctions/policy for enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors' responsibility to disclose broadly
rubrics_metrics.description: When authors submit a manuscript of any type or format they are responsible for disclosing all relationships and activities that might bias or be seen to bias their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should use the ICMJE Disclosure Form (developed to standardize disclosures); ICMJE member journals require it and others are encouraged to adopt it. Disclose relationships beyond direct support for the work where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: ICMJE Disclosure Form usage
rubrics_metrics.description: The ICMJE has developed a Disclosure Form to facilitate and standardize authors’ disclosures. ICMJE member journals require that authors use this form, and ICMJE encourages other journals to adopt it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should adopt or require a standardized disclosure form to ensure consistent, complete reporting of relationships and activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer reviewer COI duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should be asked at the time they are asked to critique a manuscript if they have relationships or activities that could complicate their review. Reviewers must disclose to editors any relationships or activities that could bias their opinions of the manuscript, and should recuse themselves from reviewing specific manuscripts if the potential for bias exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask reviewers for COI disclosure at invitation; require recusal when appropriate. Reviewers must not use knowledge of the work they’re reviewing before its publication to further their own interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor and editorial staff COI duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors who make final decisions about manuscripts should recuse themselves from editorial decisions if they have relationships or activities that pose potential conflicts related to articles under consideration. Other editorial staff members who participate in editorial decisions must provide editors with a current description of their relationships or activities (as they might relate to editorial judgments) and recuse themselves from any decisions in which an interest that poses a potential conflict exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial staff must not use information gained through working with manuscripts for private gain. Editors should regularly publish their own disclosure statements and those of their journal staff. Guest editors should follow these same procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals' special policies for editor-authored submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should take extra precautions and have a stated policy for evaluation of manuscripts submitted by individuals involved in editorial decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt transparent procedures (e.g., independent handling, external oversight) and consult COPE and WAME guidance for managing submissions from editors or staff to avoid biased handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required publication disclosures in articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles should be published with statements or supporting documents, such as the ICMJE Disclosure Form, declaring: Authors’ relationships and activities; and Sources of support for the work, including sponsor names along with explanations of the role of those sources if any in study design; collection, analysis, and interpretation of data; writing of the report; any restrictions regarding the submission of the report for publication; or a statement declaring that the supporting source had no such involvement or restrictions regarding publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear, specific statements in the manuscript or supporting materials; identify sponsors and describe any involvement or lack thereof in design, analysis, writing, or submission restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding statement content and distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of potential conflicts of interest is distinct and extends beyond direct support for this work. Within a manuscript, the funding statement should include only direct support of the work described. Support for an individual's contribution for the work should be reported as such. General institutional support for an author's time on the work should be distinguished from direct overall funding of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide granular funding information (e.g., 'This study was funded by A; Dr. F's time on the work was supported by B.'). Do not conflate institutional salary support with direct project funding without clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data access and responsibility disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the authors had access to the study data, with an explanation of the nature and extent of access, including whether access is on-going (see also Section III.L.2). To support the above statements, editors may request that authors of a study sponsored by a funder with a proprietary or financial interest in the outcome sign a statement, such as 'I had full access to all of the data in this study and I take complete responsibility for the integrity of the data and the accuracy of the data analysis.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state the level of data access and who had responsibility for data integrity and analysis; be prepared to sign attestations when sponsors have proprietary interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of participants required to disclose
rubrics_metrics.description: All participants in the peer-review and publication process—not only authors but also peer reviewers, editors, and editorial board members of journals—must consider and disclose their relationships and activities when fulfilling their roles in the process of article review and publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: COI disclosure obligations extend beyond authors to anyone participating in review, editorial decisions, or publication processes; journals should collect and publish disclosures from these groups as appropriate.
